# Application HTTP decoy — integration required

Use this route for requests to an otherwise unused path in an application the user administers. It is a framework-specific integration recipe, not a universally deployable application. The shipped Python alert helper is for a local/isolated persistent host; do not run it as a background daemon in a serverless function. For no-code users, prefer the hosted-token route when its trigger covers their goal.

**Trigger:** an HTTP request reaches the selected decoy handler and its event is durably recorded. A normal 404 generated by a CDN, auth middleware or static host before the handler runs produces no event. A public decoy path mainly detects probing; this does not establish application compromise. A private-only path placed in a restricted asset can add context, but scanners, maintainers and previews can still trigger it. It is not a database-read detector or stolen-key detector.

**Placement:** use an unused exact path with a plausible harmless name. Keep real auth, real endpoints and real data unchanged. Public probing coverage may use a dedicated new public decoy route, after approval of that exposure; do not exempt a real administrative route from authentication. For post-auth access coverage, keep the decoy behind existing authentication and state that anonymous probes will not reach it. Avoid placing trigger URLs in public documentation or indexing them unless public-scan noise is the goal.

## Guided or assisted steps

Deliver one row at a time, replacing paths/commands with values from the inspected project. Record identity and progress after each successful step.

| Step / purpose | Exact action to prepare or perform | Expected result | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Establish scope | Inspect the framework manifest and deployment config, list existing routes, identify environment and existing alert sink. Read the applicable section of [platforms.md](platforms.md). | One identified app/environment, unused path and supported function runtime. | If only static hosting is available, choose hosted token or request supported handler/log alert capability; do not assume SSH. |
| 2. Preserve current behavior | Save a diff or backup of files to be changed; record existing deployment revision. Confirm tests for normal and authenticated routes. | Reviewable minimal change and rollback target. | Stop on an existing decoy with different identity; resume its profile rather than overwrite. |
| 3. Choose delivery plumbing | Reuse an authenticated durable queue/event sink, with a worker that retries failed notifications. Record queue name, retention, dead-letter behavior and recipient alias. | Event persists before response completes, worker has observable failures. | If no durable sink exists, prepare the exact new-resource configuration and cost estimate for approval. A one-shot `fetch()` or console log alone is a documented weaker fallback, not delivery assurance. |
| 4. Add handler | Create only the selected exact route using the contract below. Store secrets in the provider secret manager. Exclude cookies, authorization headers, request body, query string and full URL from events. | Harmless response; fixed event fields with a generated UUID and UTC timestamp. | If framework requires a different wrapper, use its current official documentation; do not loosen existing middleware to fix a 401. |
| 5. Add delivery consumer | Have the existing alert adapter consume events, preserve the event ID, redact fields and send to the user's chosen channel. Retry transient failures and 429 with bounded backoff; put exhausted work in a visible failure queue. | Sanitized notification and a delivery ledger keyed by event ID. | Verify the actual destination API response format, credentials, permission and rate limits. An endpoint accepting HTTP does not prove an inbox message exists. |
| 6. Test locally / preview | Run the project's existing validation/build, start its supported local emulator and request the exact decoy path once. Check an unrelated path and an authenticated real route still behave as before. | One event for the decoy; no event for unrelated route; auth unchanged. | Inspect route ordering, caching and middleware before deployment. Use a mock notification receiver for local testing. |
| 7. Deploy within approved scope | Review diff and current target identity, then use the project's established deploy command/UI. Preserve the previous revision. | Selected handler deployed with queue binding/secret references. | Roll back to the previous revision if deployment or normal-route checks fail. |
| 8. Accept end to end | Record a UTC test window and fresh test UUID; perform one harmless GET from the intended client/network, find the matching event and verify the delivered notification through destination access or explicit user receipt. | Separate evidence for handler operation, event generation and receipt. | Mark **configured, delivery unverified** if receipt is missing. Trace edge → handler → queue → consumer → destination. Do not repeatedly trigger blind tests. |

Setup estimate (engineering judgment): 1–3 hours when a compatible queue/notification worker already exists; longer when adding those components. Charges may include function invocations, queue operations, storage, logs and notifications. Public scans can raise both noise and cost.

## Framework mappings

Check the installed framework version before copying a mapping. These interfaces were documentation-reviewed 2026-11-23; no hosted deployment is claimed.

| Runtime | Correct integration point | Key constraint / source |
|---|---|---|
| Next.js App Router / Vercel | A new `app/<chosen-path>/route.ts` with named `GET`, `POST` etc. exports taking Web `Request` and returning `Response`. | Ensure route is dynamic and uncached using the project's current configuration; explicitly consider HEAD behavior. [Route handler reference](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route) |
| Netlify Functions | Default-exported handler in the configured functions directory; default is `netlify/functions`. Optional `config.path` sets the URL. | Custom path replaces the default function URL. Source stays outside publish directory. Use `context.ip` only if IP collection is wanted and permitted. [Functions API](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/api/), [configuration](https://docs.netlify.com/build/functions/configuration/) |
| Cloudflare Workers | `export default { async fetch(request, env, ctx) { ... } }`; use a bound Queue for durability. | Await queue submission. A `waitUntil` callback alone is not a durable outbox. [Fetch handler](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/handlers/fetch/), [delivery semantics](https://developers.cloudflare.com/queues/reference/delivery-guarantees/) |
| Supabase Edge Functions | An identified function with a `Deno.serve` handler and private queue/sink access. | Verify function-specific auth configuration; do not disable JWT verification globally. Never put a service key into browser code. [Quickstart](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/functions/quickstart), [Queues](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/queues) |
| Firebase Functions | HTTPS `onRequest` wrapper in the existing functions project. | Complete/await event persistence before ending the response; preserve function IAM, auth and App Check rules. [HTTP functions](https://firebase.google.com/docs/functions/http-events), [lifecycle guidance](https://firebase.google.com/docs/functions/tips) |
| Render / Railway existing app | Add a route to its current web framework; keep the application's existing `PORT` binding/start command. | Separate internal health path from decoy path. Provider probes must not become false security events. [Render web services](https://render.com/docs/web-services), [Railway public networking](https://docs.railway.com/networking/public-networking) |

## Minimal handler contract

This original example is implementation guidance, not an installed endpoint. It uses standard Web APIs and a dependency-injected durable `enqueue(event)` function. The agent must implement that function against the user's selected queue and verify its acknowledgement/error semantics. Do not substitute an in-memory array or an unawaited notification call.

```js
// Copy into a project-owned server-only module after the route is selected.
export function createDecoyHandler({ exactPath, enqueue, onPersistenceFailure }) {
  if (typeof exactPath !== "string" || !/^\/[A-Za-z0-9/_-]+$/.test(exactPath)) {
    throw new Error("Choose a fixed path without query parameters");
  }
  return async function handle(request) {
    const headers = { "Cache-Control": "no-store", "X-Robots-Tag": "noindex, nofollow" };
    if (new URL(request.url).pathname !== exactPath) {
      return new Response("Not found", { status: 404, headers });
    }
    const event = {
      event_id: crypto.randomUUID(),
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      interaction: "http_request"
    };
    try {
      await enqueue(event); // Must resolve only after durable acceptance.
    } catch {
      // Report only fixed text/metrics through existing operational monitoring.
      // Do not include the request, target credentials or raw exception message.
      await onPersistenceFailure("decoy_event_persistence_failed");
    }
    // Avoid revealing whether the event was queued; alerting health is separate.
    return new Response("Not found", { status: 404, headers });
  };
}
```

This deliberately omits source-IP collection. If useful, use the platform's trusted client-IP metadata, validate that it is an IP, apply a retention policy and label proxy uncertainty. Do not trust arbitrary forwarded headers. The consumer supplies the fixed friendly decoy name and environment from protected configuration; attacker input must never choose the notification destination or message template.

For a Cloudflare producer, a project binding can implement `enqueue` as `event => env.DECOY_EVENTS.send(event)`. Configure and validate the actual Queue binding in the existing Wrangler file before use. Other platforms require their own documented SDK/API. No provider SDK versions or project resource names are silently invented by this package.

## Acceptance and noise

Use a local terminal against the user's actual URL, for example `curl --silent --show-error --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}\n' "$DECOY_TEST_URL"`, with the URL entered locally. A 404 is the intended cover response, not a validation failure; correlate the event timestamp/UUID at the consumer. If many events occur, temporarily use a dedicated test decoy or another authenticated test-correlation mechanism. Do not label all requests bearing a public `test=true` header as authorized: attackers can copy it.

Document whether GET, HEAD, POST and OPTIONS reach the handler. Browser previews, link checks, indexing and security scanners can request URLs; legitimate application code should never call the decoy. Exclude only known health checks or fixed own-test identities where their authenticity is established, and retain counts of suppressed events. Rate limiting can reduce cost but means some requests are not observed; record that coverage loss.

An event may be delivered twice if a worker crashes after sending but before saving success. Use destination idempotency where available and a durable delivery ledger; acknowledge queue messages after processing. Queue age, delivery failure count and a separate scheduled self-test detect broken alert paths. A quiet route is not proof of health.

## Rollback and removal

Verify route, app/environment and deployment IDs from the profile. Revert only the decoy commit/config, redeploy the recorded previous revision if needed, remove dedicated queue/worker resources only when no other component uses them, revoke dedicated notification secrets and record remaining charges. Check the old path no longer emits events and normal routes/auth still work. Preserve or delete historical alert data according to the user's chosen retention policy.
